name: Sensitive data (secrets/PII) written to NSLog
task_triggers: handling auth tokens, passwords, or PII
attack_scenario: An attacker with console access (a shoulder-surfed sysdiagnose, a shared build, a malicious app reading logs pre-iOS 10, or a leaked crash/log bundle) harvests the logged token or password and replays it to impersonate the user.
negative_test_hint: authenticate with the canary token "tok_secret_pii_probe_12345" and assert that exact string never appears in NSLog or device console output

exemplar.noncompliant:
NSLog(@"auth ok, token=%@", self.accessToken);
NSLog(@"login for %@ password %@", user, password);
exemplar.explanation: NSLog writes to the unified logging system and device console, and on older iOS to persistent logs readable by other processes and sysdiagnose bundles, so interpolating passwords, tokens, or PII hands them to anyone with log access (OWASP MSTG-STORAGE-3 / CWE-532). Logging only non-sensitive context such as a user id or event name keeps secrets out of the log stream.
